extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists, academics, and educated public interested in reviews of books, reports, and research items)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating scientific books, reports, and research items for accuracy, scholarship, readability, practical usefulness, and methodological rigor in a science-journal review format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness of literature review
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work review and cite the principal and relevant recent literature, including memoirs and short papers from the last decades?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism: the author 'passes in review the principal works ... only the titles are given, and several others are omitted altogether.' The review emphasises evidence that the author is 'quite unacquainted with the rich literature of memoirs and short papers ... within the last fifty years.' A thorough review should include recent short papers and monographs, not only classic titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy and correct attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Are factual statements correct and are discoveries/opinions attributed to the right historical figures or sources?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous concrete examples are given: mis-identifying instruments (diopter vs Jacob's staff), wrongly comparing Hipparchus' star to the new star of 1572 (when it was likely the comet of 134 B.C.), incorrect statements about the number of stars in Hipparchus's catalogue and who set the solar parallax. The reviewer expects correct factual detail and correct attribution (e.g. distinguishing Hipparchus from Ptolemy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of original (primary) sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the author consult and cite original sources rather than relying solely on secondary authorities?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review notes 'the consequences of never referring to the original sources are evident.' Reliance on secondary accounts (e.g. Duhem) without checking originals leads to omissions and perpetuation of errors; reviewers expect reference to original manuscripts/primary materials where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency and avoidance of refuted claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work avoid repeating misstatements that have been refuted by later scholarship?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the account of King Alfonso and his Tables 'reproduces all the old misstatements which have been refuted long ago.' A satisfactory work should be up-to-date and not echo long-refuted assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and completeness in technical or historical treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the account give a sufficiently detailed and accurate description of important systems, theories, or discoveries?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example criticism: Duhem's (and hence Doublet's) account of Al-Betrugi's planetary system 'misses the most important part of the system.' The reviewer expects adequate depth when treating material that was 'very much discussed' historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and consistency across chapters
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the treatment consistent in extent and quality across different sections of the work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer observes 'the author’s account ... does not differ much in extent or quality from the earlier chapters' (in a negative sense). A well-balanced book should maintain appropriate depth and quality throughout, not only in selected chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability and interest to target readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the book engaging, pleasant to read, and does it provide material likely to be new or interesting to its readers?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive note: chapters on French astronomers 'are very interesting and pleasant to read' and 'will be new to most readers.' Reviewers value readability and the ability to present novel or interesting material even if not highly technical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and appropriateness of scope/definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the subject defined clearly and is the scope appropriate (neither misleadingly narrow nor unhelpfully broad)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of McCall's book: 'Education in this book means a few of the elements of instruction, such as reading, writing, and the mechanical parts of arithmetic and composition.' A work should make clear its definitional limits and not claim to address broader topics while treating only a narrow subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical usefulness to practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the book/report provide practical guidance or tools that practitioners (teachers, growers, curators, etc.) can actually use?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: teachers would 'greatly value some help in measuring the interest of his pupils, but will ask in vain.' Fruit farming review praises inclusion of capital, land selection, law, cultural details, costings, and commercial points—practical material increases usefulness to practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test design, administration, and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: If the work addresses testing or measurement, are instructions, administration, and attempts to equalize or control for motivation and interest properly considered?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer notes 'The importance of carefully framed instructions in giving tests is rightly stressed,' but questions the prescription that 'instructions should equalize interest' as unrealistic. Guidance should address fairness, motivation effects, and realistic administration procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical rigour and proper scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Are statistical methods, test scaling, and the choice of measurement units treated rigorously and appropriately?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive comment: 'The most valuable part of the book is that concerned with “scaling the test,” as it shows the large amount of statistical treatment necessary ...' The reviewer highlights useful suggestions (e.g., common unit based on standard deviation of a reference age) and expects careful statistical treatment for measurement claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and authoritativeness of bibliography/references
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work include a comprehensive and appropriate bibliography, citing key authorities in the field?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the book provides 'useful students' bibliography,' the omission of important authors (e.g. Udny Yule) is criticised. A good scholarly work should include major, relevant references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and acknowledgement of specialist contributors / recent research
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work incorporate contributions from specialists and present recent research where appropriate, and are these contributions credited?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fruit Farming is praised because 'Many chapters have been contributed by specialists and present ... the results of recent research.' Use of specialists and up-to-date research increases authority and usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical accuracy of descriptions and explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Are technical descriptions (designs, optical principles, biological findings, etc.) correct in detail and not misleading?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Telescope is criticised for errors such as a mistaken account of how the Galilean field is determined and an incorrect description of the Dove-prism system. Technical books should avoid such mis-descriptions that could mislead practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of prose, style, and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the writing style appropriate, elegant where expected, and free from inelegant or distracting expressions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes that inelegant phrases ('credulous twaddle', 'pricked up its ears', 'blast of hot air') 'detract from the pleasure of perusal.' Stylistic matters matter for reader enjoyment and perceived authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-health/reporting policy: notification and surveillance utility
rubrics_metrics.description: For public-health reports, are notification and surveillance recommendations appropriate to enable investigation and understanding of disease?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praised policy: 'making encephalitis lethargica notifiable in 1918 ... it has become practicable to investigate each notified case and to demonstrate the general absence of personal infection from recognised cases.' Reviewers value clear surveillance measures that allow epidemiological study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epidemiological and pathological criteria for disease differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Are distinctions between diseases supported by epidemiological patterns (seasonality, age distribution), transmissibility experiments, and pathological/bacteriological evidence?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer summarises distinguishing features: encephalitis lethargica occurs in winter (Dec–Feb), poliomyelitis in late summer/autumn and chiefly in children; differences in transmissibility to animals and rarity of multiple cases; pathological and bacteriological evidence are required to separate diseases. A good report uses multiple lines of evidence to distinguish similar conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product quality assessment beyond simple sterility
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing canned food soundness, use criteria beyond mere sterility—consider whether surviving organisms can multiply and cause spoilage and which taxa are implicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the canned-meat study: 'Nearly 62 per cent. of sound tins are not sterile, the worst offenders being crab and lobster. Sterility itself is therefore not a criterion of soundness.' Guidance: assess biological characters (e.g. proteolytic ability, oxygen requirements, sporing capability) and likely behaviour under storage conditions rather than use sterility alone as the standard.
